title: Don't blame the teachers for "doing it wrong."
author: Chris O’Brien
summary: O’Brien, a former principal, argues that when a school initiative fails and leaders say staff are not doing it with fidelity, they are misdiagnosing a leadership problem as a staff problem. He frames the principal’s role, which he calls the Systemic Principal, around three verbs: design, implement and monitor. Using curriculum implementation as his running case, he shows how each verb can break down. A weak design leaves teachers without a shared picture of excellent practice, implementation without live modelling and durable artifacts leaves the design on paper, and missing walkthrough and internalization cadences let drift go unseen until the November data. The piece closes with a self-test that asks which verb each of a leader’s daily activities serves.
points: Calling low fidelity a staff failure is usually a confession that the leader never built fidelity into design, rollout or follow-up.
Adopting a high-quality curriculum is a procurement decision; implementation is a design problem that begins with leaders working the materials themselves.
Implementation is teaching, with the adults as the students: live modelling with real materials and real students, plus one-pagers and reference tools that outlast August training.
Monitoring means a fixed cadence of walkthroughs and internalization meetings tied to the standard set in design, so drift is caught in week three rather than in November data.
A practical diagnostic for principals is to ask which of design, implementation or monitoring broke down before reaching for the language of fidelity.
quotes: Done with fidelity is not a staff problem. It is a leadership one. Specifically, it is one of three leadership problems — and knowing which one matters more than almost anything else a principal can learn about their own role.
Most schools adopt a high-quality curriculum and call that the work. It isn’t. Adoption is a procurement decision. Implementation is a design problem.

Implementation is where design meets people. And people need more than a good design. They need to be walked through it — step by step, specifically, with live modeling in front of actual students showing exactly what the curriculum looks like when it’s working.
If the standard lives only in someone’s memory, it will erode. The artifact carries it when memory doesn’t.

And if every adult fails to run the curriculum as designed, you don’t blame the adults. You look at the leader. Done with fidelity as a verdict on staff is almost always a confession about implementation.
When that cadence exists, drift gets caught in week three. When it doesn’t, drift gets discovered in the November data.
